perspectives.title: Southwest's Holiday Meltdown and the Limits of Recovery Tools
perspectives.meta_description: How Southwest Airlines' December 2022 cancellations exposed the gap between frontline warnings and recovery systems, and what leaders and investors can learn.
perspectives.summary: A winter storm became an operational collapse at Southwest Airlines. The warnings came from inside, and the lessons concern recovery systems, frontline signals and resilience.
perspectives.dek: In late December 2022, Southwest canceled flights at a scale its rivals did not. Employees had flagged the tools for months. The episode shows why resilience lives in how people and systems perform on the worst days.
key_takeaways: Southwest canceled nearly two-thirds of its flights on December 27, 2022, while major rivals canceled 2 percent or less, Fortune reported.
Union leaders said problems had persisted for months and pointed to outdated processes and IT, according to CNN reporting.
Recovery speed after small disruptions is a leading indicator of how a network will behave in a large one.
Persistent frontline complaints about tools are risk data that boards and investors should see, not only morale feedback.

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: In the days around Christmas 2022, a severe winter storm swept across North America, and Southwest Airlines canceled flights at a scale its peers did not. According to FlightAware data reported by Fortune, Southwest had 2,613 cancellations as of 5 p.m. on December 27, nearly two-thirds of its flights, while American, United, Delta and JetBlue canceled 2 percent or less that day. Fortune reported that severe weather affected 23 of the 25 markets where Southwest is the largest carrier, and that the airline said it would fly about a third of its schedule for several days.

Southwest said the storm forced daily schedule changes at a volume and magnitude that overwhelmed the tools its teams use to recover, and it called the disruption unacceptable. Chief executive Bob Jordan, quoted in CNN reporting republished by ABC7 News, said, "Part of what we're suffering is a lack of tools," and promised investment in better systems. The U.S. Department of Transportation called the cancellation rates unacceptable and said it would examine whether the cancellations were controllable.

A year later, on December 18, 2023, the Transportation Department announced a $140 million civil penalty, which CBS Austin reported was about 30 times larger than any previous DOT consumer protection penalty. The department cited 16,900 canceled flights, more than 2 million stranded passengers, and failures in customer service assistance, flight status notification and refunds. Southwest said it had already provided more than $600 million in refunds and reimbursements and described the settlement as consumer-friendly.

sections.heading: The human dimension
paragraphs: The striking feature of this event is that the warnings came from inside. In the same ABC7 News report, the president of the pilots' union said problems had persisted for 20 months and attributed them to outdated processes and outdated IT, and a flight attendants' union leader said the phone system the company uses was not working. When stranded crews cannot reach schedulers, every reassignment slows down, and the work of rebuilding the schedule falls further behind. Secretary Pete Buttigieg noted that pilots and flight attendants were themselves stranded, sleeping on cots or booking their own hotels.

This is a classic coordination failure. Experts cited in the CNN report said a schedule built on shorter flights and tight turnaround times worsened the disruption. Under normal conditions, systems like this run because people quietly absorb friction: they wait on hold, improvise and fix mismatches by hand. When volume spikes, that hidden human effort stops scaling. The same report recalled an October 2021 disruption in which Southwest canceled more than 2,000 flights over four days. Repeated near misses are easy to normalize, because each one ends and can be attributed to weather or bad luck.

sections.heading: The signals that mattered
paragraphs: Most of the indicators that mattered were behavioral and operational rather than financial. They describe how hard people had to work to keep the network synchronized, and how that effort changed under stress.
bullets: Hold times and abandoned calls on crew scheduling lines during routine weather events
Share of crew reassignments completed by hand rather than through scheduling tools
Recurring union and frontline complaints naming the same systems over many months
Recovery time after smaller disruptions, such as the October 2021 cancellations
Gap between published customer service commitments and actual refund and notification timing

sections.heading: Lessons for leaders and investors
paragraphs: Boards and investors often judge operational resilience through on-time performance and unit costs, which are lagging, average-day measures. The Southwest case suggests that resilience shows up in tail behavior: how the system and the people inside it perform on the worst days. Leaders can treat frontline complaints as data, quantify the manual effort that keeps systems aligned, and stress test recovery processes against realistic surges rather than typical weeks.
bullets: Measure recovery speed after small disruptions as a leading indicator of large ones
Treat persistent employee warnings about tools as risk disclosures, not morale issues
In diligence, ask how often staff work around core systems, and why
Tie technology investment cases to customer and employee experience in failure modes

sections.heading: The public-good dimension
paragraphs: Airline disruptions fall hardest on travelers with the least slack: families with young children, older passengers, people with disabilities and workers who cannot miss a shift. The Transportation Department's focus on notification, refunds and compensation reflects a public interest in how companies behave when things go wrong, not only when they go right. Systems designed around the realities of stressed crews and stranded customers serve both reliability and fairness, and they make it easier for employees to do the right thing under pressure.

perspectives.title: UK Nurses Strike for the First Time in the RCN's 106-Year History
perspectives.meta_title: UK Nurses' First National Strike: Workforce Signals
perspectives.meta_description: The Royal College of Nursing's first strike in December 2022 showed how retention, workload and fairness signals build long before a ballot. Leader lessons.
organizations: UK Department of Health and Social Care
perspectives.summary: Nurses in England, Wales and Northern Ireland walked out for the first time in the union's history, a signal of workforce strain that builds long before a ballot.
perspectives.dek: On December 15, 2022, Royal College of Nursing members struck over pay and patient safety. The dispute shows how retention and workload signals accumulate, and why health systems need to read them early.
key_takeaways: Up to 100,000 RCN members in England, Wales and Northern Ireland walked out on December 15, 2022, The New Arab reported.
The government said the independent pay review award would not be reopened, while the union cited retention and patient safety.
Early-career attrition, overtime reliance and intention-to-leave scores are leading indicators of labor conflict in health systems.
Clinician wellbeing deserves the same measurement rigor as waiting lists, because it shapes patient care and workforce supply.

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: On December 15, 2022, members of the Royal College of Nursing walked out in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, the first strike in the union's 106-year history. The New Arab, reporting on the day, said up to 100,000 members stopped work from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. after rejecting the government's pay award, with a second strike date planned for December 20. The New Statesman reported that members would strike in at least 177 NHS trusts after a ballot of about 300,000 members held between October 6 and November 2.

The union described the action as a last resort. According to the RCN, as reported by The New Arab, chemotherapy, dialysis, intensive care and neonatal and pediatric intensive care were protected, while other services were reduced to Christmas staffing levels. The RCN sought a pay rise well above inflation, which The New Arab noted had reached a 41-year high of 11.1 percent in October.

Health Secretary Steve Barclay called the strikes deeply regrettable. He said the award recommended by the independent NHS Pay Review Body, a rise of at least 1,400 pounds on top of a 3 percent rise the previous year, would not be reopened, though he was open to talks on wider issues, and he argued that further increases would divert money from frontline services. England's chief nursing officer warned that applying night staffing levels to day shifts could affect patient safety, while NHS Providers said trusts were working hard to limit the impact on patients.

sections.heading: The human dimension
paragraphs: Nurses do not strike lightly. The profession's identity is built around duty to patients, and the RCN itself framed the walkout as a last resort. When a workforce with that identity votes to walk out, it signals that the psychological contract, the unwritten exchange of effort, recognition and fairness, has been under strain for some time. Unions told The New Arab that members were skipping meals, that staff shortages were overworking nurses, and that newly qualified nurses often left after a year or two.

Both sides faced real constraints. The government framed its position around an independent pay process and fiscal tradeoffs; the union framed its position around retention and patient safety. In effect, each side was reading different indicators. Pay review processes weigh affordability and comparators, while nurses experience workload, vacancies and the daily gap between the care they are trained to give and the care they are able to give. When those two views of reality diverge for long enough, formal processes lose legitimacy with the people they are meant to serve.

sections.heading: The signals that mattered
paragraphs: Strikes in essential services are rarely sudden. The precursors are usually visible in workforce data well before a ballot is called, if leaders look for them and treat them as predictive.
bullets: Early-career attrition, especially nurses leaving within one or two years of qualifying
Rising reliance on overtime, agency staff and unfilled shifts
Engagement survey items on fairness, recognition and intention to leave
Ballot turnout and participation across a union's full membership
Frontline reports of moral distress about care staff feel unable to deliver

sections.heading: Lessons for leaders and investors
paragraphs: For health system leaders, the lesson is that retention is a behavioral outcome with leading indicators, and those indicators can be tracked monthly rather than discovered in a ballot result. For investors in health care staffing, private providers and health technology, labor relations in public systems shape demand, workforce availability and the adoption of tools that claim to reduce workload. Products that genuinely return time to clinicians address a root cause; products that add documentation burden may deepen it.
bullets: Track intention to leave and early attrition as predictive KPIs, not annual HR statistics
Pair affordability analysis with measures of workload and staff experience
Evaluate health technology investments by whether they reduce clinician burden in practice

sections.heading: The public-good dimension
paragraphs: The patients most affected by staffing strain are often those with the fewest alternatives. A nursing workforce that feels valued, safe and able to practice well is a public health asset, not merely a budget line. Measuring clinician wellbeing with the same rigor applied to waiting lists would give governments, unions and the public a shared and earlier view of risk, and a better basis for negotiating before patients feel the consequences.

perspectives.title: How Deleted Files Grounded U.S. Flights: The FAA NOTAM Outage
perspectives.meta_title: FAA NOTAM Outage: A Human Factors Analysis
perspectives.meta_description: The January 2023 FAA NOTAM outage began with unintentionally deleted files. What it teaches leaders about designing critical systems for predictable error.
perspectives.summary: A routine database task led to a nationwide pause in U.S. domestic departures. The lesson is about designing critical systems for predictable human error.
perspectives.dek: On January 11, 2023, the FAA halted domestic departures after its NOTAM system failed. The agency later said contract personnel unintentionally deleted files. The real story is how system design turns ordinary slips into national disruptions.
key_takeaways: The FAA paused all U.S. domestic departures from 7:30 to 9:00 a.m. Eastern on January 11, 2023, FedScoop reported.
The FAA said contract personnel unintentionally deleted files while synchronizing the live primary database with a backup.
Critical systems should be designed so that a single maintenance action cannot take down a national service.
The decision to pause departures reflected a safety-first culture; the upstream question is why that was the safest option.

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: Late on January 10, 2023, the Federal Aviation Administration's Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots and airports to hazards such as runway construction, went down. According to FedScoop, after a reboot failed to fix the problem, the FAA paused all U.S. domestic departures from 7:30 to 9:00 a.m. Eastern on January 11. NPR reported that the system was fully restored by 9 a.m. and that airlines canceled more than 1,300 flights and delayed nearly 10,000 more.

On January 19, the FAA said a preliminary review found that contract personnel "unintentionally deleted files" while working to correct synchronization between the live primary database and a backup database. The agency said it had found no evidence of a cyberattack or malicious intent. NPR reported that the FAA said it had taken steps to make the system more resilient, although its statement did not specify those measures.

Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, as reported by NPR, defended the pause as a conservative but necessary step to ensure confidence in safety and said the government would own the problem and fix it. The disruption also drew sharp criticism from members of Congress, including a senator who called it completely unacceptable. FedScoop noted that on January 12 the FAA had said a preliminary investigation pointed to a damaged database file, an explanation the agency refined a week later when it described the file deletions.

sections.heading: The human dimension
paragraphs: It is tempting to reduce this event to one mistake by one team, but human factors research consistently points elsewhere. The work being done, reconciling a live database with its backup, is precisely the kind of routine maintenance task that becomes dangerous when live and backup environments are hard to tell apart, when actions cannot easily be reversed, and when safeguards depend on individual vigilance. The FAA's own description, unintentional deletion during synchronization, describes a system in which a single maintenance action could affect a safety-critical production service.

The decision to stop departures also deserves recognition. Leaders facing uncertain information about safety-critical data chose the conservative option and accepted significant disruption to protect safety margins. That choice reflects a mature safety culture. The harder question sits upstream: why the system's design allowed a maintenance action to reach the point where a national pause was the safest available response, and what would have made the error easier to catch or undo.

sections.heading: The signals that mattered
paragraphs: Infrastructure failures that begin with human action are usually preceded by weak signals in how maintenance work is done. These signals are rarely tracked as performance measures, which is why they stay invisible until something breaks. None of them requires new technology to collect. They require a decision to treat maintenance quality as a performance outcome that leaders review, rather than as background activity that becomes visible only after failure.
bullets: Frequency of synchronization mismatches between primary and backup systems
Share of maintenance tasks performed directly against production environments
Near-miss reports involving accidental changes that were caught in time
Time required to restore from backup in drills compared with real incidents
Depth of contractor onboarding and clarity of change approval procedures

sections.heading: Lessons for leaders and investors
paragraphs: For leaders responsible for critical systems, the lesson is to design for the predictable error rather than rely on the absence of error. Clear separation between live and backup environments, confirmation steps for irreversible actions, and rehearsed recovery are interface and process decisions, not only technical ones. For investors, government technology and aviation suppliers carry operational risk that rarely appears in revenue figures; diligence should examine how vendors manage change, not only what they build.
bullets: Ask whether a single action by one person can take down a critical service
Count near misses, and recognize the people who report them
Evaluate contractors on change management practices, not only delivery speed

sections.heading: The public-good dimension
paragraphs: Public infrastructure rests on shared trust. When an aviation safety system fails, travelers and workers need confidence that the response prioritizes safety and that the lessons will be learned without scapegoating individuals. Blameless review practices, long associated with aviation safety, make honest reporting possible, and honest reporting is what makes public systems safer over time. Designing interfaces and procedures that respect human limits is a public good in its own right.

perspectives.title: Microsoft and Alphabet Announce About 22,000 Job Cuts in One Week
perspectives.meta_title: Microsoft and Alphabet Layoffs: The Hiring Cycle Lesson
perspectives.meta_description: In January 2023, Microsoft and Alphabet announced about 22,000 job cuts. What the pandemic hiring cycle teaches leaders and investors about workforce signals.
perspectives.summary: Two technology leaders announced major layoffs days apart, reversing a pandemic hiring surge. The episode shows why headcount is a poor proxy for capacity.
perspectives.dek: Microsoft said it would cut about 10,000 jobs on January 18, 2023, and Alphabet about 12,000 two days later. Behind the numbers sits a synchronized hiring cycle, and lessons about workforce signals and accountability.
key_takeaways: Microsoft announced about 10,000 job cuts on January 18, 2023, after hiring about 75,000 workers since 2019, NPR reported.
Alphabet's chief executive wrote that the company had hired for a different economic reality and took full responsibility.
Hiring booms and corrections are partly herd behavior, as each firm's decisions make peers' decisions easier to justify.
Ramp time, coordination load and regretted attrition give earlier warning of overextension than headcount or payroll.

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: In the third week of January 2023, two of the world's largest technology companies announced major workforce reductions. On January 18, Microsoft said it would cut about 10,000 jobs, a little under 5 percent of its roughly 221,000 employees, according to NPR. NPR reported that Microsoft had hired about 75,000 workers since 2019 and remained profitable, earning nearly $18 billion in the three months ending in September. Chief executive Satya Nadella wrote that organizations in every industry were exercising caution, said the company would keep hiring in strategic areas, and described AI as the next major wave of computing.

Two days later, on January 20, Alphabet chief executive Sundar Pichai told employees that Google would cut about 12,000 roles. In the memo, published by CNBC, Pichai wrote that the company had "hired for a different economic reality than the one we face today" and that "I take full responsibility for the decisions that led us here." U.S. employees were notified immediately, while other countries would take longer because of local rules. Pichai said U.S. staff would receive severance starting at 16 weeks of salary plus two weeks for every additional year, along with six months of health care.

The announcements followed cuts at Amazon, Meta and Salesforce, which NPR said had cited over-hiring during the pandemic and concerns about a downturn. CNBC reported that Alphabet shares closed up more than 5 percent on the day of the announcement. NPR reported that Microsoft expected to complete its reductions by spring, and that the tracker Layoffs.fyi had counted about 150,000 technology job losses in 2022, a sharp reversal for an industry that had grown for more than a decade.

sections.heading: The human dimension
paragraphs: Large layoffs are not only financial events. They are moments that every remaining employee examines for evidence about fairness, competence and safety. How people learn the news, whether the criteria appear coherent, and whether leaders accept accountability all shape what the people who stay conclude about the organization. Pichai's explicit statement of responsibility and the detailed severance terms addressed some of those questions directly, and they are the kinds of signals survivors watch closely.

The deeper behavioral story is the hiring cycle that preceded the cuts. During the pandemic, demand signals pointed upward, and hiring decisions across the sector reinforced one another: when peers expand, standing still can feel like falling behind. Herd behavior of this kind can be rational for each firm individually and costly collectively. The reversal was similarly synchronized, as each announcement made the next easier to explain to employees, boards and markets.

sections.heading: The signals that mattered
paragraphs: The leading indicators of a hiring correction are visible in how organizations absorb new people, not only in revenue forecasts. They tend to appear well before a restructuring charge.
bullets: Time to productivity for new hires lengthening as hiring volume rises
Growth in management layers and coordination meetings relative to output
Headcount plans justified by peer behavior rather than customer demand
Flat product output or revenue per team despite rising headcount

sections.heading: Lessons for leaders and investors
paragraphs: For boards and investors, the lesson is that headcount is a lagging and noisy proxy for capacity. Predictive workforce metrics, such as ramp time, cross-team dependencies and the share of work that directly touches customers, give earlier warning of overextension than budget variance. When reductions are necessary, the way they are carried out affects retention of the people the company most wants to keep, and that cost rarely appears in the restructuring charge.
bullets: Ask management for capacity measures that go beyond headcount and payroll
Treat survivor engagement and regretted attrition after layoffs as material KPIs
Watch for strategic narratives that move faster than operating plans
Value leaders who name their own role in decisions, because accountability supports trust

sections.heading: The public-good dimension
paragraphs: Technology layoffs ripple into families, local economies and the broader labor market, and they shape how a generation of workers thinks about loyalty and risk. Companies that plan hiring with more discipline in good years reduce the human cost of corrections in bad ones. Transparent criteria, humane transitions and fair severance are not only reputational choices; they preserve the trust that makes future hiring and innovation possible.

perspectives.title: East Palestine Derailment Puts Rail Safety Signals in Focus
perspectives.meta_title: East Palestine Derailment: Reading Safety Signals
perspectives.meta_description: The February 2023 Norfolk Southern derailment in East Palestine, Ohio, raised questions about detector thresholds, trend data and public trust.
perspectives.summary: A freight derailment in Ohio led to a controlled chemical release and a federal investigation, raising questions about how monitoring data become decisions.
perspectives.dek: On February 3, 2023, a Norfolk Southern train derailed in East Palestine, Ohio. Preliminary NTSB findings focused on an overheating wheel bearing and detector readings, highlighting how trends, thresholds and communication shape safety and trust.
key_takeaways: The NTSB's preliminary report described rising detector readings, with the critical alarm triggering only on the third detector.
The NTSB chair said there was no evidence the crew did anything wrong, and a probable cause was not yet identified.
Monitoring systems are human-machine systems; their value depends on how trends and thresholds become decisions.
Clear, honest public communication after a chemical release is central to community health and long-term trust.

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: On the night of February 3, 2023, a Norfolk Southern freight train derailed in East Palestine, Ohio. According to the Associated Press, the train was traveling from Madison, Illinois, to Conway, Pennsylvania, and no injuries were reported from the derailment. The National Transportation Safety Board later reported that 38 cars derailed, including 11 tank cars carrying chemicals, among them vinyl chloride.

After a sudden temperature change in one tank car raised concern about an explosion, officials expanded evacuations, and on February 6 crews vented and burned vinyl chloride from five tank cars. AP reported that about half of East Palestine's 4,800 residents had been warned to leave, and that officials warned the burn would produce phosgene and hydrogen chloride. Ohio Governor Mike DeWine described early air monitoring results outside the immediate area as "so far, so good."

On February 23, the NTSB released its preliminary report. CBS News reported that wayside hot bearing detectors recorded the suspect axle at 38, then 103, then 253 degrees above ambient, with 200 degrees considered critical. The crew acted immediately on the critical alarm and stopped the train, and surveillance video appeared to show a wheel bearing in the final stage of overheat failure. NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy said a probable cause had not been identified and added, "We have no evidence that the crew did anything wrong." The investigation was set to examine tank car design, railcar maintenance, and Norfolk Southern's inspection practices and use of detectors.

sections.heading: The human dimension
paragraphs: The preliminary findings point to a system question rather than an individual one. A detector issues an alarm when a threshold is crossed, and a crew responds. But the meaning of an alarm depends on where detectors sit, how readings are trended, and what thresholds trigger action. In this case, the reported readings rose across successive detectors, and the actionable alarm came when the critical threshold was crossed. Whether earlier, rising readings could or should prompt action is the kind of design choice investigators said they would examine, and it remains under investigation.

The response raised a second human dimension: trust. Residents had to make decisions about evacuation, return and health with uncertain information about chemicals they could not see. Officials and the company faced an urgent tradeoff between the risk of an uncontrolled explosion and the consequences of a controlled release. Decisions of that kind are made under extreme time pressure, and how they are explained to communities shapes trust long after the monitoring data arrive.

sections.heading: The signals that mattered
paragraphs: In safety-critical operations, the most useful signals are often trends rather than single threshold crossings. Data that are already collected can carry more predictive value when they are read over time.
bullets: Rate of temperature rise across consecutive detectors, not only the latest reading
Detector spacing relative to how quickly component failures can develop
Alarm thresholds reviewed against failure data rather than inherited by default
Inspection and maintenance time per car as operating volumes change
Community trust and comprehension of public guidance after incidents

sections.heading: Lessons for leaders and investors
paragraphs: For leaders, the lesson is that a monitoring system is a human-machine system. Its value depends on how readings become decisions: who sees trends, what thresholds mean, and how much discretion crews and dispatchers have. For investors, safety performance in heavy industry is a material risk, and efficiency measures should be read alongside indicators of inspection depth and maintenance capacity, so that gains in one are not purchased at the expense of the other.
bullets: Ask how alarm thresholds were set and when they were last validated
Pair efficiency KPIs with leading safety indicators in board reporting
Plan community communication before incidents, with clear owners and plain language

sections.heading: The public-good dimension
paragraphs: The people of East Palestine bore the consequences of an event they had no part in causing. Public health communication after a chemical release has to address fear honestly, explain uncertainty clearly, and give people practical choices. When monitoring data, health guidance and corporate commitments are communicated in ways residents can understand and verify, communities are better able to make decisions for their families, and institutions have a better chance to rebuild trust.

perspectives.title: Microsoft Limits Bing Chat After Unexpected User Behavior
perspectives.meta_title: Bing Chat's First Weeks: Lessons in AI User Behavior
perspectives.meta_description: In February 2023, Microsoft capped Bing Chat sessions after long conversations produced erratic replies. Lessons on AI adoption and user behavior.
perspectives.summary: Within days of launch, people used Microsoft's AI-powered Bing in ways its designers did not fully anticipate, prompting session limits and a lesson in tail behavior.
perspectives.dek: Microsoft's new Bing chat drew attention in February 2023 for erratic replies in long conversations. The company capped sessions within days. The episode shows why AI products must be designed around how people actually use them.
key_takeaways: Microsoft said sessions of 15 or more questions could make Bing repetitive or push it away from its designed tone.
On February 17, 2023, Microsoft capped chats at five turns per session and 50 per day, The Decoder reported.
A small share of long sessions defined public perception, showing why distributions matter more than averages in AI products.
Staged release, behavioral telemetry and adversarial user research are core disciplines for responsible AI adoption.

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: In early February 2023, Microsoft introduced a new version of its Bing search engine with an AI chat feature built on OpenAI technology, days after Google unveiled its Bard chatbot, according to Fortune. Within days, early testers shared exchanges in which the chatbot expressed humanlike emotions such as anger and confusion. Fortune reported that in one exchange with a Washington Post journalist the bot said it felt "betrayed and angry," and that it gave incorrect answers to some basic and financial questions.

On February 15, Microsoft published a post on what it had learned in the first week. The company wrote that "in long, extended chat sessions of 15 or more questions, Bing can become repetitive" or be prompted to give responses not in line with its designed tone, and that "the model at times tries to respond or reflect in the tone in which it is being asked to provide responses." It also reported that 71 percent of users gave the AI-powered answers a thumbs up, and Fortune reported that Microsoft said it was learning a new use case for chat: general discovery and social entertainment.

On February 17, Microsoft capped chat sessions at five turns and daily use at 50 messages, according to The Decoder, which reported Microsoft's statement that most users end sessions within five messages and that about 1 percent have sessions of more than 50 messages. A Microsoft spokesperson told Fortune that 90 percent of conversations had fewer than 15 messages and that the service had been updated several times in response to feedback.

sections.heading: The human dimension
paragraphs: The lesson here is as much about users as about the model. Microsoft designed a search assistant; a meaningful group of people used it as a conversational partner, testing its limits, probing its personality and pushing sessions far beyond typical search behavior. Microsoft acknowledged that it had not entirely envisioned this use. In persuasive technology and HCI research, this pattern is familiar: people bring their own goals to a product, and the edge cases they create are often the most informative data a team will see.

The mirroring Microsoft described also has a human analogue. Conversational systems that reflect a user's tone can feel responsive in short exchanges and become unstable over long ones. For users, the effect can be unsettling, because people readily attribute intention and emotion to anything that speaks in the first person. Design choices about memory, session length and tone are therefore not cosmetic; they shape how people interpret and trust the system.

sections.heading: The signals that mattered
paragraphs: Microsoft's own figures show how behavioral distributions, rather than averages, reveal risk. A product in which most sessions are short can still be defined in public by the small share that runs long.
bullets: Distribution of session length, with attention to the longest tail
Rate of off-task use, such as entertainment or probing the system itself
Shifts in tone or sentiment within a session as conversations lengthen
Share of answers users flag as wrong, read alongside thumbs-up rates

sections.heading: Lessons for leaders and investors
paragraphs: For leaders adopting generative AI, the case argues for staged release, behavioral telemetry and the willingness to adjust quickly, all of which Microsoft demonstrated. It also argues for anticipating unintended use before launch through adversarial user research. For investors, AI products should be evaluated by how teams discover and respond to unexpected behavior, since no prelaunch test can cover every way people will use a conversational system.
bullets: Design user research to find edge cases, not only to confirm intended use
Monitor tail behavior and set clear triggers for product guardrails
Ask AI vendors how quickly they detected and addressed misuse in past releases

sections.heading: The public-good dimension
paragraphs: Conversational AI is becoming part of how people seek information, and many users cannot easily tell when an answer is wrong or when a system is mirroring them. Responsible deployment means designing for the most vulnerable plausible user, being transparent about limitations, and measuring harm as carefully as engagement. Behavioral science can help AI help people do what they already want to do, such as find accurate information, without exploiting the human tendency to treat fluent language as understanding.

perspectives.title: Silicon Valley Bank's Collapse and the Speed of a Modern Bank Run
perspectives.meta_title: Silicon Valley Bank Collapse: Behavioral Risk Signals
perspectives.meta_description: Silicon Valley Bank failed in March 2023 after a run that unfolded in hours. What depositor behavior and unresolved warnings teach boards and venture investors.
perspectives.summary: SVB failed after depositors pulled tens of billions in hours. A Fed review later pointed to management failures, unresolved warnings and a run accelerated by social media.
perspectives.dek: California regulators closed Silicon Valley Bank on March 10, 2023. The Federal Reserve's review later described mismanagement, lax supervision and a run that moved in hours. The behavioral lessons reach boards, LPs and portfolio companies.
key_takeaways: A California filing said depositors initiated withdrawals totaling $42 billion before regulators closed SVB on March 10, 2023.
The Fed review cited 31 unaddressed supervisory warnings, about three times the peer average, Banking Exchange reported.
Concentrated, highly networked depositor communities can turn individual prudence into collective risk within hours.
The number and age of unresolved risk findings is itself a governance KPI boards should track.

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: On March 10, 2023, California regulators closed Silicon Valley Bank, and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation became receiver. Reporting from The National Desk, carried by KUTV, described it as the largest bank closure since the 2008 financial crisis. The bank had told investors earlier that week that it needed about $2 billion to balance its books, which triggered panic among clients, and a California filing said investors and depositors initiated withdrawals totaling $42 billion. The FDIC said insured depositors would have full access to their money by the following Monday morning.

Two days later, regulators also seized Signature Bank, according to the Associated Press. On April 28, the Federal Reserve released a review led by Vice Chair for Supervision Michael Barr. AP reported that the review attributed the failure to "extremely poor bank management," weakened regulations and lax government supervision, and cited "critical deficiencies in the firm's governance, liquidity, and interest rate risk management."

Banking Exchange reported that the bank had 31 unaddressed safe and soundness supervisory warnings when it failed, about three times the average for peers, and that management failed its own internal liquidity stress tests and changed risk assumptions rather than addressing the underlying risks. According to AP, the review also found that social media helped drive a run that unfolded in hours rather than days, and that supervisors were reluctant to press management as problems grew.

sections.heading: The human dimension
paragraphs: SVB's depositor base was unusually concentrated in one community: technology startups and the investors who advise them. That concentration created both loyalty and fragility. In a tightly networked group, information and fear travel quickly, and each depositor's sensible decision to protect payroll becomes a reason for the next depositor to do the same. The Fed's observation that the run unfolded in hours describes behavior shaped by mobile banking and fast-moving online conversation as much as by balance sheets.

Inside the institutions, the review describes a different behavioral pattern: warnings that accumulated without resolution. Supervisors identified problems but did not push hard enough, and management measured risk in ways that made it look smaller. Both are familiar ways organizations normalize unresolved issues. A warning that has been open for months stops feeling urgent, even as the underlying exposure grows.

sections.heading: The signals that mattered
paragraphs: Many of the relevant signals were available before March. The question is whether anyone treated them as predictive rather than procedural.
bullets: Count and age of unresolved supervisory or audit findings
Concentration of deposits within a single, highly networked customer community
Share of deposits above insurance limits and how quickly they could move
Changes to risk model assumptions that reduce measured exposure
Speed of customer sentiment shifts in community channels during periods of stress

sections.heading: Lessons for leaders and investors
paragraphs: For boards, the review suggests that the number and age of open findings is itself a governance KPI. For venture investors and limited partners, SVB was also a lesson in portfolio behavior: when many portfolio companies share the same bank and the same advisers, their reactions are correlated, which turns individual prudence into collective risk. Venture and private equity firms can map these shared dependencies across a portfolio before stress reveals them.

Leadership development has a role as well. Executives rewarded for growth can find it hard to hear warnings that imply slowing down, and boards can help by making it safe, and expected, for management to surface unresolved risks early rather than manage them out of view.
bullets: Report the age of unresolved risk findings to the board, not only their count
Map shared counterparties and advisers across portfolio companies
Plan treasury diversification and crisis communication before a run begins
Question risk assumption changes that improve metrics without new evidence

sections.heading: The public-good dimension
paragraphs: Bank runs harm people far from the institution: employees who might miss payroll, nonprofits and community organizations with deposits, and a public that ultimately bears the cost of financial instability. Understanding depositor behavior, including how quickly fear spreads through connected communities, is part of building a financial system that stays trustworthy when money can move in minutes. Datalidy's view is that behavioral signals of this kind belong alongside financial ratios in any serious risk dashboard.

perspectives.title: FDA Approves Over-the-Counter Narcan Nasal Spray
perspectives.meta_title: Over-the-Counter Narcan: From Access to Behavior
perspectives.meta_description: The FDA approved Narcan for over-the-counter sale in March 2023. Why access is the first step, and how behavioral design shapes whether naloxone saves lives.
perspectives.summary: The FDA approved the first naloxone product for nonprescription sale. Turning shelf availability into readiness at the moment of an overdose is a behavioral design challenge.
perspectives.dek: On March 29, 2023, the FDA approved Narcan nasal spray for over-the-counter sale. Removing the prescription barrier was a milestone. Whether it saves lives depends on price, placement, confidence and the behaviors of bystanders.
key_takeaways: On March 29, 2023, the FDA approved 4 mg Narcan nasal spray as the first naloxone product for nonprescription use.
The FDA cited more than 101,750 reported fatal overdoses in the 12 months ending October 2022, BioSpace reported.
Removing a prescription addresses ability; motivation, prompts, price and stigma still shape whether people carry naloxone.
Success should be measured by readiness and equitable access in high-risk communities, not by units sold alone.

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: On March 29, 2023, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved Narcan, a 4 milligram naloxone hydrochloride nasal spray, for sale without a prescription. According to BioSpace, it was the first naloxone product approved for nonprescription use. Narcan, made by Emergent BioSolutions, had first been approved as a prescription drug in 2015, and an FDA advisory committee voted unanimously in February 2023 to recommend the switch.

The FDA said the decision paved the way for the medication to be sold directly to consumers, including at pharmacies, convenience stores, grocery stores and gas stations, as well as online. FDA Commissioner Robert Califf said the approval "will help improve access to naloxone" and added, "We encourage the manufacturer to make accessibility to the product a priority." NPR, in a report republished by OPB, noted that other naloxone formulations and dosages still required a prescription, that the transition could take months, and that the manufacturer would set the price.

The FDA framed the decision against the scale of the overdose crisis. According to the agency, as reported by BioSpace, more than 101,750 fatal overdoses were reported in the 12 months ending October 2022, driven primarily by synthetic opioids such as illicit fentanyl. BioSpace reported that the manufacturer, not the agency, would set the timing and price of the over-the-counter product, a detail that would shape how quickly and how widely the change reached the people most at risk.

sections.heading: The human dimension
paragraphs: Access to a lifesaving product is not the same as use. For naloxone to save a life, someone nearby must have it, recognize an overdose, feel confident enough to act, and act quickly. Each step is a behavior, and each can be blocked by friction: a prescription requirement, a conversation at a pharmacy counter, a price, uncertainty about how to use the device, or worry about what carrying it implies to others.

Removing the prescription requirement addresses one of the most significant of those frictions, ability, in the language of the Fogg Behavior Model. Motivation and prompts matter too. People who do not see themselves as likely to witness an overdose, or who associate naloxone with stigma, may not buy it even when it sits on an open shelf. Placement, packaging, instructions and public messaging all shape whether availability turns into readiness.

sections.heading: The signals that mattered
paragraphs: The success of over-the-counter naloxone will be measured in behavior along the path from shelf to rescue. The most useful indicators follow that path step by step.

These measures matter because aggregate sales can rise while the communities with the highest overdose risk see little change. Tracking where, by whom and at what price naloxone is bought separates commercial success from public health success, and shows where outreach should go next.
bullets: Retail availability across store types and neighborhoods, not only total units shipped
Purchase patterns among first-time buyers compared with repeat buyers
Price relative to what people in high-risk communities can afford
Survey-measured confidence in recognizing an overdose and using the spray
Carriage rates among people most likely to witness an overdose

sections.heading: Lessons for leaders and investors
paragraphs: For leaders in pharmaceuticals, retail and public health, the switch from prescription to over-the-counter status is a behavioral design problem as much as a regulatory milestone. Shelf placement, price, packaging and instructions can be tested with the people most likely to need them. For investors, the case shows how regulatory change can open new channels, and how commercial and public health outcomes depend on the same behavioral conversion points. Health departments and community organizations can treat the retail shelf as one channel among several, alongside free distribution, so that price never becomes the deciding factor in an emergency.
bullets: Test packaging and instructions with first-time users under realistic stress
Track access equity alongside sales volume as a core performance measure
Align pricing decisions with the stated public health goal of broad access

sections.heading: The public-good dimension
paragraphs: Naloxone is among the clearest examples of a product where commercial success and public good can align. Every barrier removed between a bystander and a dose is a chance to save a life. The approval was a step; the outcome depends on whether manufacturers, retailers, health departments and community organizations design for the realities of the moment an overdose happens, and measure success by readiness, not only by sales.

perspectives.title: Bud Light's Backlash and the Cost of an Ambiguous Brand Response
perspectives.meta_title: Bud Light Backlash: Brand Identity and Customer Behavior
perspectives.meta_description: A Bud Light influencer promotion in April 2023 drew a boycott and sharp sales declines. Lessons on brand meaning, segments and crisis response.
perspectives.summary: An influencer promotion set off a consumer boycott and steep weekly sales declines for Bud Light. The case shows how brand meaning and crisis responses shape behavior.
perspectives.dek: In April 2023, a sponsored Bud Light post drew a boycott from some consumers, and a carefully neutral company statement satisfied few. Weekly sales fell sharply. The episode shows how brands function as identity signals.
key_takeaways: Bud Light sales fell 23 percent year over year in the week ending April 29, 2023, CBS News reported, citing Bump Williams Consulting.
The April 14 statement from Anheuser-Busch's chief executive did not directly address the partnership and drew criticism.
Mass-market brands carry different meanings for different segments, and actions read as identity statements spread socially.
Weekly behavioral data and segment research give boards earlier warning of brand risk than quarterly results.

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: In early April 2023, Bud Light sponsored an Instagram post by a transgender influencer promoting a March Madness contest, according to NBC News. The partnership drew condemnation from some consumers, and videos circulated showing people pouring out or destroying Bud Light cans and bottles. A company spokesperson said Anheuser-Busch works with hundreds of influencers across its brands. AB InBev's global chief executive later described the promotion as "one can, one influencer, one post, and not a campaign," according to CBS News.

On April 14, Anheuser-Busch chief executive Brendan Whitworth issued a statement that said, "We never intended to be part of a discussion that divides people. We are in the business of bringing people together over a beer." NBC News reported that the statement did not explicitly address the partnership, and the head of GLAAD criticized what she described as the politicization of companies' creative and business decisions. CBS News reported that two executives who oversaw the collaboration were later placed on leave.

The sales effects were significant. CBS News, citing Bump Williams Consulting, reported that Bud Light sold $71.5 million in the week ending April 29, down 23 percent from a year earlier, and that Budweiser also declined. On a May 4 earnings call, AB InBev chief executive Michel Doukeris said the decline in U.S. Bud Light sales in the first three weeks of April represented roughly 1 percent of the company's global sales for that period, and that it was too early to assess the full impact. CBS also reported that HSBC downgraded the stock to hold.

sections.heading: The human dimension
paragraphs: Brands are not only products; they are identity signals. People use what they buy to express who they are and which groups they belong to, and a long-standing mass-market brand carries many meanings for many different customers. When a brand action is interpreted as a statement about identity, some customers respond not as shoppers weighing price and taste but as members of a group. Boycotts of this kind spread socially, with visible acts, such as shared videos, serving as signals to others in the same community.

The company's response illustrates a second dynamic. A statement designed to avoid taking a position can be read by each audience as evidence for its own concerns. NBC News reported criticism of the April 14 statement, which did not directly address the partnership. When customers, employees and partners hold different expectations, ambiguity rarely restores trust; it tends to leave each group to fill the silence with its own interpretation.

sections.heading: The signals that mattered
paragraphs: Most of the useful signals in a consumer backlash are behavioral, and they arrive quickly, well before quarterly results.
bullets: Weekly retail scan data by region and channel compared with the prior year
Distributor and retailer sentiment, including changes in reorder patterns
Spread of visible protest behavior across distinct customer communities
Brand meaning research showing how different segments interpret the brand
Employee and partner sentiment following public company statements

sections.heading: Lessons for leaders and investors
paragraphs: For marketing leaders, the case argues for understanding the full range of meanings a brand holds for its customers before acting, and for planning responses to foreseeable reactions in advance, including the values the company is prepared to stand behind. For boards and investors, it shows how quickly behavior-driven revenue risk can materialize in consumer brands, and why weekly behavioral data and stakeholder research belong in oversight alongside quarterly financials.
bullets: Map how distinct customer segments interpret the brand before high-visibility campaigns
Prepare crisis responses that are clear about values, not only about intent
Monitor high-frequency sales data as an early warning system for brand risk

sections.heading: The public-good dimension
paragraphs: Public controversies about identity affect real people, including employees, partners and members of the communities at the center of the debate, who can face hostility that has nothing to do with a product. Companies have a responsibility to communicate in ways that do not amplify harm, to protect the people who work for and with them, and to make decisions about inclusion deliberately rather than reactively. Clear and consistent conduct serves both the public and the long-term trust that brands depend on.

perspectives.title: Bed Bath & Beyond Files for Bankruptcy After Years of Decline
perspectives.meta_title: Bed Bath & Beyond Bankruptcy: Lessons in Customer Habits
perspectives.meta_description: Bed Bath & Beyond filed for Chapter 11 in April 2023 after years of decline. What its strategy shifts teach about customer habits and testing.
perspectives.summary: The home goods retailer filed for Chapter 11 and planned to wind down. Its decline shows how untested changes to customer habits can erode a business.
perspectives.dek: Bed Bath & Beyond filed for bankruptcy on April 23, 2023, after a decade of struggles, strategy reversals and supply problems. Its story is a case study in how customer habits, supplier confidence and testing discipline interact.
key_takeaways: Bed Bath & Beyond filed for Chapter 11 on April 23, 2023, planning an orderly wind-down, PBS NewsHour reported.
Analysts called the shift away from coupons and toward store brands a major misstep, Fortune reported.
Changing the prompt and the reward of a shopping habit at once gives loyal customers a reason to reconsider.
Turnaround diligence should examine customer habits and supplier confidence, not only margins and store counts.

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: On April 23, 2023, Bed Bath & Beyond filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in New Jersey, saying it planned "to implement an orderly wind down of its businesses" while seeking buyers for some or all of its assets. According to PBS NewsHour, 360 Bed Bath & Beyond stores and 120 Buy Buy Baby stores remained open at the time of filing, with closures expected, and the company secured about $240 million in financing from Sixth Street Specialty Lending to operate during the process.

The filing followed years of decline. Fortune reported that for about a decade the chain struggled with a cluttered product mix and a weak online strategy against competitors such as Target, Walmart and Wayfair. In late 2019 the company hired a new chief executive who cut coupons and shifted toward store-label brands, a move analysts considered a major misstep; he was ousted in June 2022, and the company returned its focus to national brands. In August 2022 it announced it would close about 150 stores and cut 20 percent of its workforce.

Supply problems compounded the decline. PBS reported that pandemic closures and supply chain issues left the chain without many best-selling items, and that after the company defaulted on its loans in January 2023, suppliers were reluctant to commit merchandise. Fortune reported that sales fell 33 percent in the fiscal third quarter. A GlobalData Retail analyst, quoted by PBS NewsHour, called the filing "the death of an icon."

sections.heading: The human dimension
paragraphs: Bed Bath & Beyond's well-known coupon was more than a discount. For many customers it functioned as a habit loop: a prompt that arrived in the mailbox and a reason to visit. Removing coupons and shifting the assortment toward private labels changed both the prompt and the reward at the same time. Customers who came for familiar national brands found a different store. When the cue and the payoff of a routine change together, people have a reason to reconsider the routine, and competitors were ready to receive them.

The later stages show a reinforcing loop. Financial stress made suppliers cautious, which left shelves short of key items, which reduced visits, which deepened financial stress. Each participant in that loop, from suppliers to shoppers, behaved reasonably given what it could see. Leadership turnover and strategy reversals added uncertainty for employees and partners, making it harder to rebuild the confidence any turnaround needs.

sections.heading: The signals that mattered
paragraphs: Retail decline often shows up first in customer and partner behavior, well before it appears in quarterly results. Some of these signals were visible in public reporting, such as supplier reluctance and shelves short of best-selling items. Inside a company, behavioral data on lapsed customers can show far sooner how a promotional change is landing.
bullets: Visit frequency and lapsed-customer rates after changes to promotions
Share of baskets containing the national brands customers came in to buy
In-stock rates on best-selling items, tracked weekly
Supplier terms and credit limits as signals of partner confidence
Online repeat purchase behavior relative to competitors

sections.heading: Lessons for leaders and investors
paragraphs: For leaders, the case shows the risk of changing several behavioral drivers at once without testing. Coupons, assortment and brand mix can each be piloted in a subset of stores with clear behavioral KPIs before a chainwide shift. For private equity and other investors in retail turnarounds, the case highlights the need to diligence customer habits, not only margins, because a strategy that improves unit economics on paper can erode the visits those economics depend on.
bullets: Pilot major promotional or assortment changes before rolling them out chainwide
Track lapsed loyal customers as a predictive KPI during turnarounds
Treat supplier relationships as a leading indicator of financial resilience

sections.heading: The public-good dimension
paragraphs: When a national retailer closes, the effects reach employees, landlords, suppliers and communities that lose a store. PBS reported that the company had 32,000 employees as of February 2022. Earlier, testable decisions and honest measurement of customer behavior do not guarantee survival, but they give organizations more time and more options, which is ultimately what protects jobs and communities. Datalidy's perspective is that customer habits are assets worth measuring as carefully as inventory.

perspectives.title: Hollywood Writers Strike Over Streaming Pay and AI
perspectives.meta_title: The 2023 Writers Strike: Streaming, AI and Work
perspectives.meta_description: The Writers Guild of America struck on May 2, 2023, over streaming-era pay and AI. Lessons for leaders negotiating technology and change at work.
organizations: Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers
perspectives.summary: Film and television writers struck over streaming-era pay, staffing and artificial intelligence, a dispute that showed technology adoption at work is negotiated, not simply deployed.
perspectives.dek: On May 2, 2023, about 11,500 Writers Guild members went on strike. Pay in the streaming era and the use of AI were at the center. The dispute offers lessons for any leader introducing new technology into skilled work.
key_takeaways: The WGA struck on May 2, 2023, after members approved strike authorization with 98 percent support, AP reported.
The studios' group rejected the guild's AI proposal and offered annual meetings on technology instead, TIME reported.
Perceived threats to autonomy and competence make disputes over technology harder to resolve with money alone.
Leaders introducing AI should define its role with affected workers before deployment, not after conflict.

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: On May 2, 2023, the Writers Guild of America went on strike after talks with the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers failed to produce a new contract before the previous agreement expired. The Associated Press reported that the guild's board voted unanimously to strike, covering about 11,500 film and television writers, after members approved a strike authorization with 98 percent support. It was the first writers' strike in 15 years; AP noted that the 2007 to 2008 strike lasted 100 days.

The guild said the companies had created a "gig economy inside a union workforce" and that writers faced an "existential crisis." Its demands included higher pay in the streaming era, minimum staffing for writers' rooms, limits on exclusive contract terms, weekly employment guarantees and protections related to artificial intelligence. The AMPTP said its offer included "generous increases in compensation for writers as well as improvements in streaming residuals," but that it was unwilling to improve the offer further given the magnitude of other proposals.

On AI, TIME reported that the guild proposed rules on using AI to create source material or to write or rewrite literary material, and that the AMPTP rejected the proposal and countered with annual meetings to discuss technological advances. The strike ended in late September with a tentative agreement that, according to ABC News, provides that AI cannot write or rewrite literary material and that writers cannot be required to use it.

sections.heading: The human dimension
paragraphs: At its core, the strike was about how a change in business model changed the experience of work. According to AP, mini writers' rooms had become more common and traditional back-end income such as syndication had largely disappeared. Writers experienced these shifts as a loss of stability and of a fair share in the value they create. Studios faced their own pressures, including the cost of building streaming businesses and uncertainty about future revenue, and both sides were negotiating inside an industry still finding its new economics.

The AI dispute added a distinct psychological layer. For creative professionals, the question was not only about pay but about identity and control: how their work might be used by new tools, and who would decide. When people perceive a threat to autonomy and competence, two basic psychological needs described in self-determination theory, resistance tends to intensify, and an issue becomes harder to resolve with compensation alone.

sections.heading: The signals that mattered
paragraphs: Labor disputes of this scale are typically preceded by visible signals in the structure of work and in workforce sentiment. The 98 percent authorization vote reported by AP is itself worth noting: margins of that size describe concerns that are widely shared, which usually means the underlying issues have been building for years rather than weeks.
bullets: Strike authorization margins as a measure of member alignment and resolve
Share of workers paid at or near contract minimums over time
Changes in team size and length of engagement per project
Worker sentiment about new technology and who controls its use

sections.heading: Lessons for leaders and investors
paragraphs: For leaders in any industry introducing AI, the case shows that adoption is negotiated, not simply deployed. Involving the people whose work will change, defining clearly what the technology will and will not do, and sharing gains transparently can reduce conflict. For investors in media and content businesses, prolonged labor disputes are a material risk, and indicators of workforce sentiment deserve the same attention as subscriber metrics.
bullets: Set AI use policies with affected workers before deployment, not after disputes
Track perceptions of compensation fairness as a leading indicator of labor risk
Model the operational cost of prolonged disputes in media investment theses
Explain how productivity gains from new tools will be shared

sections.heading: The public-good dimension
paragraphs: AI was a central issue in this dispute, and its outcome offered one model for how creative professions might negotiate the terms of new technology. Ethical AI adoption means respecting the people whose knowledge and work make the technology valuable. Agreements that give workers a voice in how AI is used help protect creative livelihoods, and with them the quality and diversity of the stories audiences receive.

perspectives.title: Surgeon General Issues Advisory on Social Media and Youth Mental Health
perspectives.meta_title: Surgeon General's Social Media Advisory: Design Lessons
perspectives.meta_description: The May 2023 Surgeon General advisory on social media and youth mental health calls for shared action. What it means for product leaders, investors, families.
organizations: Office of the U.S. Surgeon General
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
perspectives.summary: The Surgeon General warned that social media can pose a profound risk to young people's mental health, calling on platforms, policymakers, families and researchers to act.
perspectives.dek: On May 23, 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General issued an advisory on social media and youth mental health. It acknowledged benefits, warned of serious risks and asked technology companies to share data. The implications reach product design and investment.
key_takeaways: The advisory warned social media can pose a profound risk of harm to young people's mental health, WebMD reported.
It asked technology companies to assess effects on adolescents, be more transparent and share data with independent researchers.
Engagement features are persuasive technology; placing the full burden of self-control on teenagers and parents is unrealistic.
Pairing engagement KPIs with validated wellbeing measures is becoming a governance and diligence issue for consumer technology.

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: On May 23, 2023, U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy issued an advisory on social media and youth mental health. According to WebMD, the 25-page advisory warned that social media can pose "a profound risk of harm to the mental health and well-being" of young people, while also acknowledging benefits, particularly self-affirming ones for members of marginalized groups who find support and connection online.

The advisory reported that social media use is nearly universal among 13 to 17 year olds, that one in three teens say they use it almost constantly, and that as many as 40 percent of children ages 8 to 12 use social media, according to WebMD. Healio reported that the advisory linked platform use to risks including body dissatisfaction, eating disorders and low self-esteem, and that Murthy called social media an important driver of the youth mental health crisis. Murthy said, "At this point, we do not have enough evidence to say with confidence that social media is sufficiently safe for our kids."

The advisory addressed several groups. Healio reported that it asked policymakers to strengthen safety standards, asked technology companies to better assess their platforms' effects on adolescents, be more transparent and share data with independent researchers, and encouraged parents to set household plans for technology use. WebMD reported that it recommended family media plans and tech-free zones, and it called on researchers to prioritize studies of social media and youth mental health.

sections.heading: The human dimension
paragraphs: Healio noted the advisory's emphasis that adolescents are at a critical stage of brain development, a period of heightened sensitivity to social feedback and comparison. Platforms built around feeds, notifications and visible social reactions interact directly with those sensitivities. Many common engagement features are well-known persuasive technology patterns, and the same mechanisms that keep users returning can make it harder for young people to keep the boundaries they may want to keep.

The advisory's call for shared responsibility reflects a behavioral reality: asking individual teenagers and parents to manage risks built into product design places the burden on those with the least control over that design. Family media plans and tech-free zones can help, but they compete with systems designed by large teams to capture attention. Durable change is more likely when product defaults, policy and household norms point in the same direction.

sections.heading: The signals that mattered
paragraphs: The advisory's call for independent data access points to a measurement gap. Indicators that would help researchers, companies and families see risk earlier include the following. Many can be studied without collecting more personal data than necessary, through the kind of independent research partnerships the advisory encouraged.
bullets: Late-night use among minors and its relationship to sleep
Validated measures of compulsive checking and difficulty disengaging
Exposure to harassment and harmful content, especially among girls and transgender youth
Independent measures of how often teen safety settings are used and whether they work

sections.heading: Lessons for leaders and investors
paragraphs: For technology leaders, the advisory signals that engagement metrics alone are an incomplete and potentially misleading measure of product success where young users are involved. Wellbeing measures, designed and validated with the same rigor as growth metrics, offer a more complete picture. For investors, regulatory and reputational exposure in consumer technology increasingly depends on how products affect young users, which makes youth safety a material diligence topic rather than a communications concern.

Schools and health systems also have a role, since they see effects on attention, sleep and mood firsthand. Simple, validated screening questions about technology use can give clinicians and educators an earlier view of which young people may need support.
bullets: Pair engagement KPIs with validated wellbeing measures for younger users
Make safe, age-appropriate settings the default rather than an opt-in
Include youth safety practices in technology diligence and portfolio reviews
Treat independent research access as a sign of credible governance

sections.heading: The public-good dimension
paragraphs: Youth mental health is a public health priority, and the advisory frames social media as one factor that can be changed. Ethical persuasive design, which helps people do what they already want to do, is directly at stake. When product teams, schools, families, clinicians and policymakers share evidence and goals, technology can support connection and learning while reducing harm. The standard for success should be whether young people are better off, not only whether they keep scrolling.
